text.p: Tiger Woods tackled Royal Troon for the first time on Monday accompanied by about 400 spectators and four marshals charged with keeping the crowd at bay.
But the "minders" had little to do as the young American favourite took on the potentially troublesome Western Scottish links where the British Open starts on Thursday.
"We're basically crowd beaters but we hope we won't have to beat up any crowds," one of the marshals said before Woods began.

Michael Bonallack, secretary of the organising Royal and Ancient Club, said the marshals' job "was to make sure the people don't badger him too much so he can concentrate on golf and not have to sign autographs all the time".
Bonallack said that a police officer might be assigned to Woods later in the week.
Woods, whose achievements have been startling since he turned professional late last summer, was not out to humble the course on his first visit.
Playing with close friend and Florida neighbour Mark O'Meara, John Cook and Dudley Hart, the world number one went gently about the process of learning the 7,079-yard layout.
With a slight wind behind, Woods might have tried his luck at driving the first few greens on the relatively easy opening holes, but he spurned the opportunity.
His tee shot at the 364-yard first finished in rough some 40 yards short of the green.
At the 391-yard second and the 379-yard third, he used an iron off the tee for safety -- a significant clue to his plan of attack.
He found more rough off the tee at the 557-yard fourth and his escape shot landed short of the green and took a sharp bounce left.
Woods was preparing for his third British Open. He was still an amateur when he finished joint 66th at St Andrews and joint 22nd at Royal Lytham last year.
